subtitle: Start from zero
description: Your first real English: the structures every sentence uses, practised out loud in small conversations.

themes.title: Language-exchange café
themes.subtitle: Meet and greet
themes.situation: You are at a friendly language-exchange café. Meet the learner, exchange names, countries and jobs using the verb to be.

themes.title: Nice to meet you
themes.subtitle: Start somewhere small
themes.situation: Meet the learner for the first time. Learn their interests through natural introductions.

lessons.title: The verb “to be”
lessons.goal: Introduce yourself and ask simple questions with am/is/are.

explanation: Every English sentence needs a subject and a verb. The most important verb is “to be”. It tells you what someone is, how someone feels, or where something is.
One verb, three present forms. With I use am: “I am Ana.” With you, we and they use are: “You are my friend.” With he, she and it use is: “She is a doctor.”
In everyday talk, English shortens it: I'm, you're, he's, she's, it's, we're, they're. When you chat, say “I'm Ana”, not “I am Ana”.

examples.text: The café is near the station.

expressions.note: With your name, age or feeling: I'm Ana. I'm tired.
Never “I from …” — the am is obligatory.
Are you a student? Are you tired?

expressions.text: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
expressions.meaning: Short answers to an Are-you question.

expressions.note: He's a teacher — the a matters with professions.

expressions.meaning: The fixed phrase when you meet someone.

lessons.situation: You meet someone new at a friendly language-exchange café. Introduce yourselves and ask simple questions with the verb to be.

questions.prompt: Hello! I'm Ana. What's your name?
questions.watch: Answering only the name without the verb: accept it, then recast with “I'm …”.

questions.prompt: Where are you from?
questions.watch: “I from Spain” — recast “I am FROM Spain”, stress am.

questions.prompt: Are you a student?
questions.watch: “Yes, I student” — the short answer needs am.

questions.prompt: How are you today?
questions.watch: “I fine” — recast “I'm fine”.

questions.prompt: Is your city big or small?
questions.watch: “My city big” — recast “My city IS big”.

questions.prompt: We're friends now! Where is your family from?
questions.watch: “My family from …” — recast with is.

exercises.explain: With he, she and it, to be becomes is.
With they, to be is always are.
Am goes with I: I am from …

exercises.prompt: Introduce yourself in one sentence: say your name.
exercises.explain: I'm Ana / My name is Ana — the verb is never dropped.

lessons.title: Questions & negatives with “to be”
lessons.goal: Ask yes/no and wh- questions, and say what is not true, with am/is/are.

explanation: To ask a yes/no question, put the verb first. “You are tired.” becomes “Are you tired?” “She is a teacher.” becomes “Is she a teacher?”
To say something is not true, add not. “I am not late.” In talk we shorten: is not → isn't, are not → aren't. And I'm not is already short.
Real questions add question words: what, where, who, how. They go before the verb: “Where are you from?” Short forms: what's = what is, where's = where is.

expressions.note: Are you OK? Are you new here?

expressions.meaning: Say what is not true about you.
expressions.note: I'm not from Madrid — I'm from Seville.

expressions.meaning: Say what is not true about others.
expressions.note: She isn't here. They aren't at home.
Where's the station? Where are my keys?

lessons.situation: You chat with a new neighbour in the lift. Ask simple questions and say what is and isn't true for you.

questions.prompt: Hi! Are you new in the building?
expected: No, I'm not. I'm on the third floor.
questions.watch: “Yes, I new” — short answers repeat am.

questions.prompt: Is your flat big?
questions.watch: “No, it not big” — the negative is isn't.

questions.prompt: I'm Marta, by the way. What's your name?
questions.watch: “What you name?” — the question needs is: “What's your name?”.

questions.prompt: Where are you from?
questions.watch: “Where you from?” — don't drop are.

questions.prompt: Are your neighbours friendly?
questions.watch: “Yes, they friendly” — repeat are.

questions.prompt: I'm not from this city — I'm from Valencia. And you?
questions.watch: “I no from …” — the negative is “I'm not from …”.

exercises.explain: With you, the question starts with Are.
With she, questions start with Is.

exercises.prompt: Ask where the person is from.

exercises.explain: I'm not is already short; is not → isn't, are not → aren't.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.goal: Give a complete self-introduction: name, age, country, nationality and job.

explanation: A good introduction answers five small questions: your name, your age, your country or city, your nationality, and your job.
In English, age and nationality use the verb to be. “I'm 30.” “I'm Mexican.” Say “I'm 30”, never “I have 30”.
With jobs we say a/an: “I'm a nurse.” “He's an engineer.” Nationality words are adjectives: from Spain → I'm Spanish; from Mexico → I'm Mexican.

expressions.meaning: Adjective with be: Spanish, Turkish, Brazilian.
Your job. Use an before a vowel sound.
The polite answer to “Nice to meet you”.
expressions.note: Same smile, one extra word: too.

lessons.situation: First day in class: the teacher asks everyone to stand up and introduce themselves to two classmates.

questions.prompt: Good morning! Please introduce yourself.
questions.watch: One line is fine — the tutor will ask for more.

questions.prompt: Lovely to meet you. How old are you?
questions.watch: “I have 25” — age uses be: “I'm 25”.

questions.prompt: Where are you from?
questions.watch: “I'm Spanish from Spain” — keep it simple: “I'm from …”.

questions.prompt: So you're from Italy — you're Italian, right?
questions.watch: “I'm Italy” — the country is Italy, the person is Italian.

questions.prompt: What's your job?
questions.watch: “I'm teacher” — jobs need a/an: “I'm a teacher”.

questions.prompt: Great! Now introduce your friend: this is Carlos.
questions.focus: talking about a third person with is
questions.watch: “Carlos is teacher” — add a: “a teacher”.

exercises.explain: With I, always am — even in short answers.
The fixed greeting is Nice to meet you.
Never “I from …” — the am is obligatory.

exercises.prompt: Say your name and your job.
answers: My name is <name> and I'm a <job>
exercises.explain: Use a before jobs: a teacher, a doctor.

themes.title: Family photo album
themes.subtitle: Who's who
themes.situation: You show the learner a family photo album. Name the people, ask about each other's families and say who has what.

themes.title: The lost jumper
themes.subtitle: Whose is it?
themes.situation: A jumper appeared in the classroom. Help find its owner: ask what things are, whose they are and what they look like.

lessons.title: a/an, the & plurals
lessons.goal: Talk about one thing, a specific thing and many things.

explanation: Use a or an for one of many — any one. Use an before a vowel sound: a book, an apple, an hour.
Use the when the listener knows exactly which one. First we introduce with a/an (“I have a cat”), then we talk about it with the (“The cat is old”).
For more than one, most words take -s: book → books. After -s, -sh, -ch, -x we add -es: bus → buses, watch → watches. A few are special: person → people, child → children.

expressions.meaning: One of many; an before a vowel sound.
Special plurals: person → people, child → children.

lessons.situation: You help at a small shop on market day: count things, name things and ask for one specific item.

questions.prompt: Welcome! Can I help you?
questions.watch: The first time you name a thing: a/an, not the.

questions.prompt: This one here on the shelf? The blue one?
questions.watch: “Yes, blue one” — keep the: “the blue one”.

questions.prompt: How many bags do you need?
questions.watch: “two bag” — plural needs -s: “two bags”.

questions.prompt: Do you want apples or oranges?
questions.watch: “three orange” — add -s.

questions.prompt: The watches are over there. How many do you need?
questions.watch: “two watchs” — after ch it's “watches”.

questions.prompt: Is your family big?
questions.watch: “four persons” — say “people”.

exercises.explain: An before vowel sounds: an idea, an hour.

exercises.prompt: Look at ___ sun. It is hot.
exercises.explain: There is one sun, so use the.
Plural jobs take no article: they are teachers.

exercises.prompt: Complete with two things: I need a ___ and an ___.
exercises.explain: a + consonant sound, an + vowel sound.

lessons.title: This / that & my / your
lessons.goal: Point at things near and far, and say who they belong to.

explanation: Use this for something near you, that for something far from you both. Plurals: these (near) and those (far).
Possessive words go before the thing: my, your, his, her. “This is my bag.” “That's your coat.” “Her name is Ana.”
To ask about the owner: “Is this your …?” or “Whose is this?” The answer repeats the owner: “It's mine.” / “No, it's his.”

expressions.meaning: Ask if it belongs to the listener.

lessons.situation: You and the learner arrive early to class and find bags, phones and coats on the tables: identify what's near, what's far, and who owns what.

questions.prompt: Good morning! Is this your bag on the chair?
questions.watch: “Yes, is my bag” — English needs it: “Yes, it's my bag”.

questions.prompt: And this phone? Whose is it?
questions.watch: “It's of Ana” — no of: “It's mine”.

questions.prompt: Look at the board — do you see those words?
questions.watch: “this words” for far things — use “those”.

questions.prompt: I'm holding two keys. Are these your keys?
questions.watch: “this keys” — plural near is “these keys”.

questions.prompt: Is that your bike outside?
questions.watch: Far away: that, not this.

questions.prompt: Whose gloves are those on the floor?
expected: I don't know. They aren't mine.
questions.watch: “They is mine” — plural: “they're mine”.

exercises.prompt: ___ is my bag. Here, in my hand.
exercises.explain: This points at something near you.
That points at something far away.

exercises.prompt: Point at something near you and say what it is.

lessons.title: “Have got”: family
lessons.goal: Say who is in your family and what you have, with have got.

explanation: have got = have. Use it for family, pets and things: “I've got two sisters.” “She's got a dog.” With he/she/it use has got.
Questions flip it: “Have you got any brothers?” Negatives add not: “I haven't got a car.” “He hasn't got time.”
Family words: mother and father (parents), brother, sister, son, daughter, grandmother and grandfather (grandparents). In talk: mum, dad, grandma, grandpa.

examples.text: My parents have got a small dog.

lessons.situation: You swap family photos: describe your family, ask about the learner's, and compare what you both have.

questions.prompt: Tell me about your family — have you got brothers or sisters?
questions.watch: “I have two brother” — plural -s and got: “I've got two brothers”.

questions.prompt: Have you got any pets?
expected: No, I haven't got any pets.
questions.watch: “Have you got some pets?” — questions use any.

questions.prompt: Has your mum got a car?
questions.watch: “Yes, she got” — short answers repeat has.

questions.prompt: Are you the oldest, the youngest or in the middle?
questions.watch: “I am more old” — “the oldest”.

questions.prompt: Have your parents got a garden?
expected: Yes, they have. They've got flowers.
questions.watch: “They has got” — plural takes have.

questions.prompt: I've got a big family — six of us! And you?
questions.watch: “We is five” — “we are five”.

exercises.prompt: Say how many brothers or sisters you have got.
answers: I haven't got any brothers or sisters

themes.title: The morning rush
themes.subtitle: Against the clock
themes.situation: It's 7:40 and you both have somewhere to be. Describe your morning routine while the clock runs.

themes.title: After work
themes.subtitle: The quiet hours
themes.situation: It's the end of the day. Tell each other what you do in the evening and how you unwind.

lessons.title: Present simple: I / you / we / they
lessons.goal: Talk about routines and facts with I/you/we/they, and ask with do.

explanation: The present simple is for habits and facts: “I work in a bank.” “We live near the park.” With I, you, we and they the verb has no ending.
Questions and negatives use do: “Do you like coffee?” “I don't eat meat.” The main verb goes back to its simple form.
Short answers repeat do: “Do you speak English?” — “Yes, I do.” / “No, I don't.”

expressions.text: Yes, I do. / No, I don't.

lessons.situation: Two neighbours chat in the square about their week: jobs, habits and what they never do.

questions.prompt: So, what do you do?
questions.watch: “What you do?” — questions need do.

questions.prompt: Do you like your job?
questions.watch: “Yes, I like” — short answer is “Yes, I do”.

questions.prompt: Where do you work?
questions.watch: “I work in home” — “from home”.

questions.prompt: Do you speak any other languages?
questions.watch: “I no speak” — “I don't speak”.

questions.prompt: What do you and your friends do at weekends?
questions.watch: “We plays” — with we there's no -s.

questions.prompt: I don't watch much TV. Do you?
questions.watch: Short answers use do, not the verb.

exercises.explain: With they there is no -s: they live.

exercises.prompt: Say you do not eat meat.
exercises.explain: don't + base verb: We don't eat.

exercises.prompt: Say one thing you do every day.
exercises.explain: Present simple for routines: I work, I walk, I cook.

lessons.title: He / she / it + -s & frequency
lessons.goal: Describe another person's routines with the -s ending and say how often things happen.

explanation: With he, she and it the present simple verb takes -s: “She works at night.” “He likes jazz.” This -s is small but very important.
Questions and negatives use does: “Does she live here?” “He doesn't drive.” After does the verb loses its -s: not “Does she works?”
Frequency words say how often: always, usually, often, sometimes, never. They go before the verb: “I always walk to work.” But after be: “He is never late.”

lessons.situation: You catch up about a mutual friend: describe her routines, how often she does things and what she never does.

questions.prompt: Tell me about your best friend — where does she live?
questions.watch: “Where does she lives?” — after does, no -s.

questions.prompt: What does he do at weekends?
questions.watch: “He play” — he needs -s: “He plays”.

questions.prompt: Does she like football?
questions.watch: “Yes, she likes” — short answer: “Yes, she does”.

questions.prompt: How often do you cook?
questions.watch: “I cook two times week” — “twice a week”.

questions.prompt: Is your brother always late?
questions.watch: “He always is late” — after be: “He's always late”.

questions.prompt: My sister never drinks coffee — she hates it. And your family?
questions.watch: “My mum never drink” — keep the -s after never.

answers: My sister works in a cafe

lessons.title: Time & daily routine
lessons.goal: Tell the time and describe your day in order.

explanation: Ask with “What time is it?” Answer with o'clock for exact hours: “It's seven o'clock.” For halves say half past: “It's half past seven” (7:30).
Use at for clock times (“at eight”), in the morning/afternoon/evening, and at night.
Order your day with first, then, after that and finally. They make a story out of your routine.

examples.text: I get up at six thirty.
First I shower, then I dress.
Finally, I go to bed at eleven.

expressions.note: Opposite: I go to bed at …

lessons.situation: The learner's first day at a new job: plan the morning together, minute by minute, from waking up to the first meeting.

questions.prompt: Quick — what time is it?
questions.watch: “Is seven o'clock” — statements need it's.

questions.prompt: What time do you get up?
questions.watch: “I get up in seven” — clock times take at.

questions.prompt: Do you have breakfast before or after your shower?
questions.watch: Answer in order: first …, then …

questions.prompt: What do you do in the evening?
questions.watch: “in the night” — evening or “at night”.

questions.prompt: When do you go to bed?
questions.watch: “I go to the bed” — no the: “go to bed”.

questions.prompt: Describe your morning in order — first, then, after that.
expected: First I …, then I …, after that I …
questions.watch: Use the order words — don't list with “and, and, and”.

exercises.explain: Clock times take at: at seven.

exercises.prompt: Say what comes after getting up.
Say what time you usually get up.

themes.title: A new neighbourhood
themes.subtitle: Find your way
themes.situation: The learner just moved to the area. Walk the streets together and describe what there is on every corner.

themes.title: Lost in town
themes.subtitle: Ask for help
themes.situation: Your phone died and you are lost. Stop people, ask for directions and follow them.

lessons.title: Can / can't
lessons.goal: Say what you are able to do, ask others for help and give permission.

explanation: can never changes: “I can swim.” “She can swim.” No -s, no to. The negative is can't (or cannot in writing).
Questions flip it: “Can you swim?” For polite requests: “Can you help me?” For permission: “Can I sit here?”
Short answers repeat can: “Yes, I can.” / “No, I can't.”

expressions.note: I can drive, but I can't park!

lessons.situation: You organise a small trip with the learner: who can drive, who can cook, and what you can't do without asking.

questions.prompt: Can you drive?
questions.watch: “Yes, I drive” — repeat can: “Yes, I can”.

questions.prompt: What can you cook?
questions.watch: “I can to cook” — no to after can.

questions.prompt: Can your sister swim?
questions.watch: “She cans swim” — can never takes -s.

questions.prompt: Can I borrow your pen, please?
questions.watch: Answer a request warmly: “Of course”.

questions.prompt: Sorry, can you speak more slowly?
questions.watch: Practise your “Sorry, can you …?” — it opens every repair.

questions.prompt: What's one thing you can't do but want to learn?
expected: I can't <skill>, but I want to learn.
questions.watch: “I can't to play” — no to after can't.

exercises.prompt: I ___ swim, but I can't dive.
exercises.explain: can never takes -s and stays with the verb.
can't + base verb: She can't drive.

exercises.prompt: Ask permission to open the window.
answers: Can I open the window, please

lessons.title: There is / there are
lessons.goal: Say what exists in a place, and ask about it.

explanation: To say something exists, start with there: “There's a pharmacy on the corner.” Singular: there is (there's). Plural: “There are two parks.”
Negatives: “There isn't a lift.” “There aren't any shops.” Questions: “Is there a bank near here?” “Are there any tickets left?”
Say where with prepositions: next to, opposite, behind. “The café is next to the bank.”

examples.text: The bank is opposite the school.

expressions.meaning: Ask for a number of things.

lessons.situation: You show a visitor around the office building: what's on each floor, what's missing, and where exactly things are.

questions.prompt: Is there a supermarket near your flat?
questions.watch: “Is a supermarket?” — start with there.

questions.prompt: How many rooms are there in your home?
questions.watch: “How many rooms has?” — with there: “are there”.

questions.prompt: Is there a lift in the building?
expected: No, there isn't. It's an old building.
questions.watch: “Yes, has lift” — repeat there is.

questions.prompt: What's in your neighbourhood?
questions.watch: One thing → there's; more → there are.

questions.prompt: Are there any good cafés around?
questions.watch: “There aren't some cafés” — negatives take any.

questions.prompt: Where exactly is the pharmacy?
questions.watch: “It's in front the bank” — “opposite” or “in front of”.

exercises.prompt: There ___ two parks in my neighbourhood.
Say that a market exists on Saturdays.
answers: There is a market on Saturdays

exercises.prompt: Say what there is in your kitchen.
exercises.explain: There is + one thing, there are + many.

lessons.title: Directions & place
lessons.goal: Give and follow simple directions from A to B.

explanation: Start with go straight on, then turn left or turn right. “Go straight on and turn left at the lights.”
Say where the place is: on the left, on the right, on the corner, at the end of the street.
Ask for directions with “How do I get to …?” or “Is it far?” Answers: “Five minutes on foot.”

examples.text: How do I get to the station?
Go straight on for two streets.

expressions.text: on the left / on the right
expressions.note: The pharmacy is on your left.

lessons.situation: The learner's phone has died at a crossroads: ask passers-by for the museum, understand the directions and repeat them back.

questions.prompt: You look lost — can I help?
expected: Yes, please. How do I get to <place>?
questions.watch: Start with “Excuse me” — it buys goodwill.

questions.prompt: OK: go straight on and turn left at the lights. Got it?
expected: Straight on, then left at the lights.
questions.watch: Repeat the route back to check it.

questions.prompt: Is the museum far from here?
questions.watch: “It has five minutes” — “it's five minutes”.

questions.prompt: When you leave, the pharmacy is on your right.
questions.watch: “in the right” — sides take on.

questions.prompt: Where's the nearest metro station?
expected: Go straight on and it's on the corner.
questions.watch: Give order words: straight, then turn.

questions.prompt: Perfect. One last thing — is there a toilet in the museum?
expected: Yes, there is, on the left.
questions.watch: Tie it together: there is + place word.

exercises.explain: Exact points take at: at the lights.
Question word + is: Where is / Where's.

themes.title: The rainy window
themes.subtitle: Weather small talk
themes.situation: You both watch the rain from a café window. Describe the weather and what people are doing outside.

themes.title: The busy kitchen
themes.subtitle: What is happening now
themes.situation: You are cooking together. Say what everyone is doing right now — and who is doing nothing!

lessons.title: What is happening now
lessons.goal: Describe actions happening at this moment with am/is/are + -ing.

explanation: For actions happening right now, use am/is/are + verb-ing: “I am reading. She is cooking. They are playing.”
The -ing never changes: I am eating, you are eating, he is eating. Only am/is/are changes.
Spelling: make → making (drop the e), sit → sitting (double the consonant after one short vowel).

expressions.note: It is always it for weather.

expressions.meaning: Point at an action in progress.

lessons.situation: You look out of a busy café window with a friend: say what every person outside is doing at this moment.

questions.prompt: Look at Tom — what is he doing? (football)
questions.watch: “He playing” — the is never drops: “He's playing”.

questions.prompt: What are you doing right now?
questions.watch: “I read” is a habit; right now it's “I'm reading”.

questions.prompt: What's the weather like at this moment? (rain)
questions.watch: “Is raining” alone has no subject — weather needs it.

questions.prompt: And your friends? (wait for us)
questions.watch: “They waiting” — plural needs are.

questions.prompt: Is Maria working today?
questions.watch: “Yes, she working” — repeat is in the short answer.

questions.prompt: Say two things you are not doing right now.
questions.watch: “I not reading” — the negative is “I'm not reading”.

exercises.explain: Right now needs am/is/are + -ing: she is writing.
It is raining — weather takes it.

exercises.prompt: Say what they are doing. (TV / watch)

exercises.explain: make drops the e; sit doubles the t.

lessons.title: Asking about now
lessons.goal: Ask and answer present-continuous questions, and say what is not happening.

explanation: Questions flip the verb: “You are listening.” → “Are you listening?” “She is coming.” → “Is she coming?”
Negatives add not: “I'm not working today.” “He isn't coming.” “They aren't sleeping.”
Question words go first: “What are you doing?” “Where is she going?” “Who are you calling?”

examples.meaning: Short answer, then the real action.

expressions.note: I'm not eating meat this week.

lessons.situation: You phone a friend who is at a party: ask what is happening, who is doing what, and what people are not doing.

questions.prompt: Your friend answers the phone. Ask what she is doing.
questions.watch: “What you doing?” — informal speech drops are, but learn the full form.

questions.prompt: Ask if Tom is coming to the cinema.
expected: Is Tom coming to the cinema?
questions.watch: “Tom is coming…?” needs a question mark of order: “Is Tom coming…?”

questions.prompt: Say you are not drinking coffee these days.
questions.watch: “I no drinking” — English says “I'm not drinking”.

questions.prompt: Ask where your guests are going now.
questions.watch: “Where they going?” — keep are: “Where are they going?”

questions.prompt: Is the baby sleeping? (no)
questions.watch: “No, baby not sleeping” — “No, the baby isn't sleeping”.

questions.prompt: Ask who is making that noise.
questions.watch: “Who making” — who needs is: “Who is making…?”

exercises.explain: With you, the present-continuous question starts with Are.
is not → isn't: She isn't working today.

exercises.prompt: Answer with a full sentence: What are you wearing today?
exercises.explain: I'm wearing + clothes — wear is almost always continuous.

lessons.title: The weather today
lessons.goal: Talk about today's weather and what people are wearing.

explanation: Weather uses it: “It's cold. It's raining. It isn't sunny.” Ask: “What's the weather like?”
Wear lives in the continuous: “I'm wearing a coat.” “She's wearing a hat.”
Two present tenses, two jobs: habits use present simple (“It often rains here”), right now uses continuous (“It's raining now”).

examples.text: It often rains here, but today the sun is shining.

lessons.situation: You are planning a walk with a neighbour: ask about the weather, describe what you are wearing and decide what to take.

questions.prompt: A neighbour opens the door. Ask about the weather.
questions.watch: “How is the weather?” also works; “What's the weather like?” is the classic.

questions.prompt: Describe a perfect beach day. (two adjectives)
questions.watch: “Is sunny” — weather needs it: “It's sunny”.

questions.prompt: It started to rain. What do you say? (verb)
questions.watch: “It rains now” is a habit form; right now is “It's raining”.

questions.prompt: Ask what your friend is wearing today.
questions.watch: “What do you wear?” asks about a habit.

questions.prompt: Say what you are wearing right now.
questions.watch: “I wear a coat” sounds like every day — right now is “I'm wearing”.

questions.prompt: Your friend has no coat and it's cold. Give advice.
questions.watch: “You take a coat” is fine but the natural shout is “Take a coat!”

exercises.explain: The fixed question is What's the weather like?
wear in the continuous: is wearing.

exercises.prompt: It's 35 degrees and the sun is out. Describe the weather (one sentence).
exercises.explain: It's + weather adjectives: hot and sunny.

themes.title: The birthday plan
themes.subtitle: Which day works?
themes.situation: You are planning a small birthday dinner. Compare days, fix a date and divide the tasks.

themes.title: At the pharmacy
themes.subtitle: Not feeling well
themes.situation: You have small health problems. Say how you feel, what hurts and what you need.

lessons.title: Days, months & dates
lessons.goal: Say the days of the week, months and dates, and make appointments.

explanation: Days and months are always capital letters: Monday, May. The week starts with Monday in the UK, Sunday in the US.
Use on with days (on Monday), in with months and years (in June, in 2026), and at with times (at three o'clock).
Dates: “My birthday is on 5 May” — say “the fifth of May”. Ordinals: first, second, third… twenty-first.

lessons.situation: You and a classmate want to study together: compare your weeks, pick a day and a time, and put it in the calendar.

questions.watch: “See you in Saturday” — days take on.

lessons.title: Free time and hobbies
lessons.goal: Talk about hobbies with play, go and do, and say how often.

explanation: Three verbs own the hobbies: play for games (play football), go for -ing activities (go swimming), do for the rest (do yoga).
Say how often with adverbs: always, usually, often, sometimes, never — they go before the main verb: “I often swim.”
Ask back: “What do you do in your free time?” “Do you play any sports?”

lessons.title: Follow the instructions
lessons.goal: Give and follow instructions with imperatives, and politely ask people to do things.

explanation: The imperative is the verb alone: “Open the box. Listen carefully. Turn left.” It works for instructions, directions and recipes.
Negatives use don't: “Don't touch it. Don't worry.”
Soften with please and let's: “Please sit down.” “Let's start.” Let's = a suggestion for both of us.

examples.text: Don't touch the pan — it's hot!

expressions.note: The verb alone is the command.
Please can go first too: Please sit down.

questions.prompt: The class is noisy. What does the teacher say? (quiet)

lessons.title: How do you feel?
lessons.goal: Describe feelings and small health problems, and ask about other people.

explanation: Feelings use be: “I'm tired. She's happy. They're hungry.” Health problems use have got: “I've got a headache.”
Ask: “How are you feeling?” “What's wrong?” Answer: “I don't feel well.” “My leg hurts.”
Small comfort: “Get better soon!” “Take care!”

lessons.goal: Buy tickets and ask about buses and trains: times, platforms and prices.

lessons.goal: Describe how you travel to work or school with by + transport.

explanation: by + transport for the means: “by bus, by train, by car, by bike, by plane”. On foot for walking: “I go to work on foot.”
The question: “How do you get to work?” Answers add a time: “It takes twenty minutes.”
get to + place = arrive: “I get to the office at nine.” get home — no to: “I get home at six.”

explanation: Supermarket words come in groups: the fruit section, the dairy section, the frozen food aisle.

Say needs with need + noun: “We need rice, eggs and tomatoes.”

lessons.title: Small talk
lessons.goal: Chat politely with strangers: the weather, the weekend and friendly exits.

explanation: Small talk has safe topics: the weather, the weekend, the neighbourhood. Politics and salary are not small talk.
The rhythm: comment + question. “Cold today, isn't it? Do you know if the bus is late?”
Exit kindly: “Well, have a good one!” — you don't need a reason to stop.

lessons.title: Asking for help
lessons.goal: Ask strangers for help in a shop or street, and thank them properly.

explanation: Open with excuse me: “Excuse me, where's the lift?” It signals a request is coming.
Requests with can: “Can you help me?” “Can I ask something?” After help, say thank you + a follow-up.
If you don't understand, say so: “Sorry, can you repeat that?” — people are kind about it.

lessons.goal: Name the places in a town and say what there is near you.

explanation: Town places: a bank, a bakery, a chemist's, a library, a park, a school. With a/an the first time: “There's a bakery near my house.”
there is / there are do all the work: “There's a park. There are two schools.” Negative: “There isn't a cinema.”
Ask back: “Is there a bank near here?” — near here is the magic phrase.

lessons.goal: Say what your town is like with adjectives and because.

lessons.goal: Talk about likes and dislikes with love, like, don't like and hate.

explanation: The pattern: subject + love/like/don't like/hate + noun or verb-ing: “I love music.” “She likes dancing.”

Strong words: love is 100%, like is warm, don't like is polite, hate is strong — use hate for fun, carefully.

Times and places finish the plan: “At eight, at the main square.” A plan without a place is a wish.

lessons.title: Some / any & countables
lessons.goal: Talk about food quantities: what you have, what you need and how much.

explanation: Countable things have a plural: one apple, two apples. Uncountable things have no plural: water, rice, milk, bread.
Use some in affirmative sentences (“We've got some rice”) and any in questions and negatives (“Have we got any milk?” “There isn't any bread.”).
To count uncountables, add a container: a bottle of water, a kilo of rice, a loaf of bread.

To soften, add really or quite: “I really love singing.” “I don't really like getting up early.”

explanation: The magic order phrase is “I'd like …” (I would like) — polite and universal. “Can I have …, please?” works everywhere too.

lessons.title: Was / were
lessons.goal: Describe people, places and feelings in the past with was and were.

explanation: Was and were are the past of to be. I/he/she/it → was. You/we/they → were. “I was at home.” “They were at the beach.”
Negatives: wasn't, weren't. Questions flip: “Was it good?” “Where were you?”
Anchor the story in time: yesterday, last night, last week, in 2020, this morning.

expressions.meaning: Give your verdict of the past.

lessons.situation: You bump into a friend who missed the neighbourhood party on Saturday: recount who was there, how it was and what wasn't good.

questions.prompt: Where were you on Saturday?
questions.watch: “I were at home” — with I use was.

questions.prompt: Was the party fun?
questions.watch: “Yes, was fun” — keep it: “Yes, it was”.

questions.prompt: Were there many people?
questions.watch: “There was many” — plural: “there were”.

questions.prompt: How was the music?
questions.watch: “It were good” — it takes was.

lessons.title: Past simple: -ed
lessons.goal: Tell what you and others did, with regular past forms and didn't.

explanation: For finished actions, regular verbs add -ed: work → worked, play → played, watch → watched. The same form works for every person.
Questions and negatives use did + plain verb: “Did you walk?” “I didn't walk.” After did, no -ed: not “Did you walked?”
Spelling: love → loved (no e), study → studied (y→ied), stop → stopped (double p).

expressions.text: Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.

lessons.situation: You compare diaries from a chaotic Tuesday: what you did, what you didn't do, and what the other did first.

questions.prompt: What did you do yesterday evening?
expected: I watched TV and cooked dinner.
questions.watch: “I watch TV” — past answer needs -ed: “I watched”.

questions.prompt: Did you sleep well?
questions.watch: The short answer repeats did: “Yes, I did”.

questions.prompt: Did you walk to work?
questions.watch: “I didn't walked” — after didn't, plain verb.

questions.prompt: What time did you finish work?
questions.watch: “What time did you finished?” — after did, plain finish.

questions.prompt: Did you study English last week?
expected: Yes, I did. I studied on …

exercises.explain: After didn't the verb stays in base form.

exercises.prompt: Say they got here late yesterday.

lessons.title: Your weekend (repaso)
lessons.goal: Tell the story of your weekend in order — past be, past verbs, time anchors — and ask about someone else's.

explanation: A weekend story has three parts: where you were (was/were), what you did (past -ed), and how it was (was + opinion).
Order it with time anchors: on Saturday morning, then, in the evening, later, finally.
Keep the conversation alive: ask back with “What about you?” or “Did you …?”

examples.text: On Friday I was at home — I was exhausted.
On Saturday I visited my parents.
We walked in the park and talked for hours.
In the evening I watched a film.
It was a really good weekend.

questions.watch: Start with the verdict, then the story.

questions.watch: Use -ed for regular verbs and an order word.

lessons.title: Comparatives
lessons.goal: Compare two things with -er/more … than.

explanation: Short adjectives take -er: cheap → cheaper, big → bigger, busy → busier. Long adjectives take more: more expensive, more comfortable.
The comparison word is than: “This flat is cheaper than that one.” “The kitchen is bigger than the bedroom.”
Irregulars: good → better, bad → worse, far → further.

examples.text: This café is cheaper than that one.
Trains are more comfortable than buses.
My flat is bigger than yours.
This book is better than the film.
Is the market cheaper than the supermarket?

expressions.meaning: The two irregulars you need most.

questions.prompt: Compare two flats: the second one is modern, the first isn't. (sentence)
expected: The second flat is more modern than the first.
questions.watch: “moderner” doesn't exist — long adjectives take more.

questions.prompt: The bus takes 40 minutes, the train takes 25. Compare them.
expected: The train is faster than the bus.
The bus is slower than the train.
questions.watch: Keep than in the sentence: “faster than”.

lessons.title: Superlatives
lessons.goal: Say which one is the most / the -est in a group.

explanation: Short adjectives: the + -est: the cheapest, the biggest, the busiest. Long adjectives: the most + adjective: the most beautiful.
Superlatives live with in or of: “the cheapest café in town”, “the best day of the year”.
Irregulars: good → the best, bad → the worst.

examples.text: It's the cheapest café in town.
That's the most beautiful street here.

It's the oldest building in the neighbourhood.

questions.watch: Superlatives need the: “the cheapest”, never just “cheapest”.

questions.prompt: Describe a very famous place in your country. (long adjective)

questions.watch: “the famousest” doesn't exist — the most famous.

questions.prompt: Which is correct: “the best” or “the most good”?
questions.watch: good → the best, bad → the worst.

lessons.title: Object pronouns
lessons.goal: Use me, you, him, her, it, us and them after verbs and prepositions.

explanation: After a verb, use the object pronoun: “Can you help me?” “I saw her yesterday.” “Call them later.”
After prepositions too: “with me”, “for him”, “without them”, “between us”.
it stays it; you stays you. Subject does the action, object receives it: “She loves him.”

examples.text: I saw them at the market.

expressions.meaning: with me, for him, to her.

expressions.note: Between you and me — never “between you and I”.

questions.watch: “Let me to help” — let takes the bare verb.

questions.prompt: Say you saw Anna and Tom at the cinema. (them)

questions.prompt: Your friend is carrying bags. Offer to carry one. (it)
expected: Can I carry it for you?

questions.watch: Never “between you and I” — after a preposition use me.

lessons.title: Going to: plans
lessons.goal: Talk about future plans and intentions with am/is/are going to.

explanation: Plans use be + going to + verb: “I'm going to visit my family. She's going to study tonight. We're going to move house.”
Questions flip be: “Are you going to come?” Negatives add not: “I'm not going to work on Saturday.”
going to is about intention — a plan already in your head. Time markers: tonight, tomorrow, next week, this weekend.

examples.text: I'm going to learn to cook.
She's going to start a new job.
We're going to travel in June.
Are you going to watch the match?
I'm not going to pay for that!

expressions.note: Are you going to join us?

expected: What are you going to do at the weekend?

questions.watch: “I going to travel” — be comes first: “I'm going to”.

questions.watch: Present evidence → going to: “It's going to rain”.

expected: I'm not going to stay out that late.

answers: she's going to start a course

lessons.title: Irregular past verbs
lessons.goal: Tell past stories with the most common irregular verbs.

explanation: Many common verbs are irregular: go → went, see → saw, make → made, take → took, come → came, get → got.
Negatives and questions return to the base form with did: “I didn't go. Did you see it?” The past lives only in the positive.
Learn them in pairs: buy → bought, eat → ate, drink → drank, write → wrote, drive → drove, sleep → slept.

examples.text: We went to the coast last summer.
She made a cake for my birthday.
He came home late and went to bed.

expressions.note: I saw it, I took it.

I didn't sleep well — not “didn't slept”.

questions.watch: “I goed / I wented” — the irregular is went.

questions.prompt: Say you didn't sleep well last night.
expected: I didn't sleep well last night.
questions.watch: “didn't slept” — after didn't, the verb is bare: sleep.

expected: Did you see the news yesterday?
questions.watch: “Did you saw” — after did, base form: see.

questions.prompt: Tell one thing you made this week. (make)

lessons.title: Advice & obligation
lessons.goal: Give advice with should and talk about rules with must and have to.

explanation: should = good idea, advice: “You should rest. You shouldn't work tonight.” It never takes -s or to.
must = obligation from the speaker; have to = obligation from outside (rules, timetables): “I must finish this.” “I have to wear a uniform.”
Questions: “Should I call him?” “Do you have to work on Sundays?” Negatives: “You shouldn't smoke.” “I don't have to get up early.”

examples.text: She has to wear a uniform.
Do we have to book a table?

expressions.note: I have to work on Saturdays.

expected: I must take the medicine every day.

lessons.title: How much / how many
lessons.goal: Ask about countable and uncountable things with how much and how many.

explanation: Countable things (bottles, rooms, tickets) take many: “How many rooms do you need?” Uncountable stuff (water, money, time) takes much: “How much water do you need?”
In everyday questions, much alone sounds formal: “How much money?” is fine, but people say “How much is it?” — the full countable question needs many.
Answers use a lot of / some / a few (countable) / a little (uncountable): “We need a few chairs and a little luck.”

examples.text: How much milk is in the fridge?
We need a few more chairs.
A lot of people are coming.

expressions.note: a lot of rooms, a lot of water.

lessons.title: Sending messages
lessons.goal: Write short informal messages: plans, apologies and quick questions.

explanation: Messages drop the formal bits: “Running late — 10 mins!” No “Dear”, no full sentences every time. But clarity stays: who, what, when.
Useful message chunks: “On my way!” “Are we still on for…?” “Can we move it to…?” “Sorry, something came up.”
Emoji-free writing still matters: punctuation carries tone. “Fine.” sounds angry; “Fine :)” sounds fine.

lessons.title: Describing symptoms
lessons.goal: Explain what hurts and for how long at the doctor's.

explanation: Symptoms use have got: “I've got a headache / a sore throat / a temperature.” Pain uses hurt: “My back hurts.”
Duration with for + present perfect: “I've had this cold for three days.” The doctor asks: “How long have you had it?”
Severity helps the doctor: “It's a sharp pain.” “It's worse when I move.”

lessons.title: Friendly advice
lessons.goal: Give and respond to advice about health and habits with should.

explanation: Advice with should: “You should sleep more.” “You shouldn't check your phone in bed.” Never should to.
Soften advice with maybe and try: “Maybe you should try going to bed earlier.” try + -ing for experiments.
Accept or decline: “You're right, I'll try.” “I know, I know… it's hard!” Advice between friends is a dance.

examples.text: You shouldn't drink coffee at night.
Maybe you should try walking home.
I know, I know… it's hard!
You should see a doctor if it lasts a week.

lessons.situation: A friend has been tired for weeks: hear the symptoms, give three pieces of advice with should and one with try + -ing, and agree on a first step.

questions.prompt: Give advice about screens at night. (shouldn't)
expected: You shouldn't use screens at night.
questions.watch: shouldn't + base verb: no to.

questions.prompt: Give softer advice: walking after lunch. (try)
expected: Maybe you should try walking after lunch.
questions.watch: try + -ing for the experiment.

questions.prompt: Accept the advice.
questions.watch: I'll try — promise an attempt.

questions.prompt: Close the advice with a check.
questions.watch: see if it helps = a ver si funciona.

expected: You should see a doctor if the pain continues.

Maybe you should try ___ before ten. (sleep)

answers: You shouldn't drink coffee at night

lessons.title: Habits: then and now
lessons.goal: Compare old and new habits with used to and now, and say what changed.

explanation: Old habits with used to: “I used to sleep eight hours.” New ones with now + present: “Now I sleep five.” The contrast tells the story.
Frequency still works: “I hardly ever exercise now.” hardly ever = almost never — softer than never.
Be honest about difficulty: “It's harder than I thought.” than + the comparison.

examples.text: I used to sleep eight hours.
My weekends used to be active. Now they're for the sofa.

expressions.note: I used to run every day.

lessons.situation: You compare your student life with your working life: sleep, exercise, food — used to for the past, now for the present, and one new habit you've started.

questions.prompt: Say an old exercise habit. (run every day)
expected: I used to run every day.
questions.watch: used to + base verb.

questions.prompt: Say the present: no time now.
questions.watch: now + present simple.

questions.prompt: Say you almost never cook these days.
expected: I hardly ever cook these days.
questions.watch: hardly ever = casi nunca.

questions.prompt: Say one new habit you've started. (walking to work)
questions.watch: I've started + -ing: the new habit.

questions.prompt: Say your weekends used to be active.
expected: My weekends used to be active.
questions.watch: used to + verbo base.

exercises.prompt: I ___ to run every day when I was a student.
I ___ ___ ever cook these days. (casi nunca)
Say your new habit. (started / I've / walking / to work)
Compare: sleep eight hours before, five now.
answers: i used to sleep eight hours now i sleep five

themes.title: The bucket list
themes.subtitle: Have you ever…?
themes.situation: You compare life experiences: places you have and haven't been, things you have and haven't tried.

themes.title: Story night
themes.subtitle: What was happening?
themes.situation: You tell a story with background: what was happening when something unexpected occurred.

lessons.title: Present perfect: experiences
lessons.goal: Talk about life experiences with have/has + past participle, without saying when.

explanation: Experiences without a time use have/has + past participle: “I've visited Rome. She's never tried sushi. Have you been to Japan?”
The moment you say WHEN, switch to past simple: “I've been to Rome. I went there in 2019.”
Participates are irregular often: be → been, see → seen, go → gone/been, eat → eaten, do → done.

examples.text: She's seen that film three times.
I've already packed, but I haven't printed the tickets.

expressions.note: Reply: Yes, I have / No, I haven't.

expressions.meaning: gone = still there; been = visited and returned.
expressions.note: She's gone to Rome (not back yet).
I've been to Peru. I went in 2018.

lessons.situation: You meet a traveller at a hostel: swap life experiences with Have you ever…? and ask follow-up questions with past simple when they give a when.

questions.prompt: Ask a traveller if they have ever visited Japan.
expected: Have you ever been to Japan?
questions.watch: “Did you ever visit…?” is possible in AmE, but “Have you ever…?” is the safest form.

questions.prompt: Answer negatively: you have never tried surfing.
questions.watch: “I've never tried to surf” changes meaning slightly; keep “tried surfing”.

questions.prompt: Say you visited Rome in 2019 (mention the year).
questions.watch: “I've gone to Rome in 2019” — a finished time forbids the present perfect.

questions.prompt: Your friend is not here — she went to the airport. Say it two ways.
expected: She has gone to the airport.
questions.watch: “She's been to the airport” means she went and came back.

questions.prompt: Say you have seen that film three times.
expected: I've seen that film three times.
I have seen that film three times.
questions.watch: “I saw it three times” needs a past anchor; without one, prefer the present perfect.

questions.prompt: Ask a follow-up when someone says “I've been to Iceland”.
questions.watch: The follow-up asks about the trip → past simple.

exercises.explain: With a finished time (in 2018), use past simple.

lessons.title: Past continuous: background
lessons.goal: Set the scene of a past story with was/were + -ing, and interrupt it with past simple.

explanation: Background actions use was/were + -ing: “It was raining. People were running. I was cooking.”
The classic structure: past continuous (background) + when/until + past simple (event): “I was cooking when the lights went out.”
Two parallel background actions use while: “While she was sleeping, he was reading.”

examples.text: The sun was setting and the birds were singing.
I was cooking when the phone rang.
They were waiting for the bus when it started to rain.
While we were driving, it snowed.
What were you doing at midnight?

expressions.note: While I was waiting, I read.

expressions.text: It was a normal evening when…

lessons.situation: You and a friend swap short stories: set the scene with past continuous, then deliver the surprise event with past simple.

questions.prompt: Set the scene: the rain / fall, and people / run for shelter.
expected: The rain was falling and people were running for shelter.
questions.watch: “The rain fell” is an event — the background is “was falling”.

questions.prompt: Add the interruption: you were cooking / lights went out.
expected: I was cooking when the lights went out.
questions.watch: The short event takes past simple: “went out”, not “was going out”.

questions.prompt: Ask what your friend was doing at ten last night.
expected: What were you doing at ten last night?
questions.watch: “What did you do at ten?” asks for an answer list; “were doing” asks about the moment.

questions.prompt: Say two parallel actions: you drove / your partner read the map.
expected: While I was driving, my partner was reading the map.
questions.watch: Both long actions take the continuous after while.

questions.prompt: Open a story: normal evening / everything changed.
expected: It was a normal evening when everything changed.
questions.watch: Background first (was), event second (changed).

questions.prompt: Negative background: you weren't listening when she told you.
expected: I wasn't listening when she told me.
questions.watch: “I didn't listening” — negatives of the continuous use wasn't/weren't.

exercises.prompt: I ___ dinner when the doorbell rang.
Ask about a past moment. (you / at midnight / what / were / doing)
answers: What were you doing at midnight

exercises.prompt: Fix: “While I cooked, she was watching TV.”
answers: while i was cooking she was watching tv
exercises.explain: Both parallel long actions take the continuous: was cooking.

lessons.title: Used to: past habits
lessons.goal: Compare the past with now using used to / didn't use to.

explanation: Past habits that stopped use used to + verb: “I used to play outside every day. She used to live in Berlin.”
Negative: didn't use to: “We didn't use to have a car.” Question: “Did you use to…?” Note: no -d in the negative/question.
For states still true, prefer present simple; for single past events, past simple. used to is for repeated past routines that ended.

examples.text: I used to hate coffee. Now I love it.
There used to be a cinema here.
We didn't use to lock the door.
Did people use to write letters?
He didn't use to cook — now he's a chef!
I used to walk to school.

expressions.note: Did you use to play an instrument?
I used to walk, but now I cycle.
There used to be a lake here.
I'm used to getting up early.

lessons.situation: You look at old photos with a friend: compare childhood habits with life now using used to, didn't use to and but now.

questions.prompt: Say one childhood habit you have stopped.
questions.watch: “I used to played” — used to + base verb.

questions.prompt: Say something about your town that no longer exists. (There used to…)
expected: There used to be a market here.
questions.watch: “There used to have” is wrong — use be for places/things.

questions.prompt: Say you didn't like vegetables before.
expected: I didn't use to like vegetables.
I used to not like vegetables.
questions.watch: Careful spelling: didn't use to (no -d).

questions.prompt: Ask a friend about an old habit. (instrument / sport)
expected: Did you use to play an instrument?
Did you use to do any sport?
questions.watch: “Did you used to…?” — in questions, use to loses the -d.

questions.prompt: Contrast: past walk to school, now cycle.
expected: I used to walk to school, but now I cycle.
questions.watch: The contrast word now makes the change explicit.

questions.prompt: Say you are accustomed to early mornings. (be used to)
expected: I'm used to getting up early.
questions.watch: Different structure: be used to + -ing = estar acostumbrado.

exercises.prompt: She ___ live in Berlin when she was young.
Ask about old habits. (you / use / play / did / to / an instrument)
answers: Did you use to play an instrument
exercises.explain: Did + you + use to + base verb.

exercises.prompt: Fix: “I'm used to get up early.”
answers: i'm used to getting up early
i am used to getting up early

lessons.title: Writing your story
lessons.goal: Turn an experience into a short written story with a beginning, a turn and an ending.

explanation: Written stories breathe: short sentences for tension, long ones for scenery. Start in the middle: “The lock wouldn't turn.”
Spine: opening moment → the turn (when/until/suddenly) → the ending feeling. Three paragraphs, 80-120 words.
Show, don't label: not “it was a bad day” but “my keys, my phone and my umbrella were all on the kitchen table — together, at home, where I wasn't.”

examples.meaning: Open in the middle of the trouble.

examples.text: It started fine: sun, coffee, an early train.
Until the announcement, everything was normal.
By the time I got home, I'd laughed about it twice.
Some days you're the tourist, even in your own city.

expressions.note: By the time + past, past perfect feels natural.
Some days you win, some days you learn.

lessons.situation: You write a 100-word story for the class blog: a travel day that went wrong — opening in the middle, one turn, one closing thought.

questions.prompt: Open your story in the middle of the trouble. (the lock)
questions.watch: “Last summer I travelled…” is a report, not a story.

questions.prompt: Set the calm before: sun, coffee, an early train.
expected: It started fine: sun, coffee, an early train.
questions.watch: A calm first line makes the turn hit harder.

questions.prompt: Signal the turn: the announcement changed everything. (until)
expected: Until the announcement, everything was normal.
questions.watch: until + noun/clause marks the exact turn.

questions.prompt: Add pace: the platform emptied suddenly. (short sentence)
questions.watch: One-word openers (Suddenly, Luckily) control pace.

questions.prompt: Close with distance and humour.
expected: By the time I got home, I'd laughed about it twice.
questions.watch: Distance turns disaster into story.

questions.prompt: Add a one-line reflection to close.
expected: Some days you're the tourist, even in your own city.
questions.watch: One line, not a moral lecture.

exercises.prompt: Which opening starts IN the trouble?
options: Last summer I travelled a lot.
It was a sunny day in June.
I want to tell you about trains.
exercises.explain: In medias res: start inside the problem.

exercises.prompt: ___ the doors closed, we realised the mistake.
Write a one-line closing thought for a travel disaster story.
answers: some days you're the tourist even in your own city
some days you win some days you learn
at least i have a story now

themes.title: Plan B
themes.subtitle: If it rains…
themes.situation: Your outdoor plan is at risk. Negotiate conditionals: if this happens, we'll do that.

themes.title: The film debate
themes.subtitle: Which one? However…
themes.situation: You review a film together: describe scenes with relative clauses and connect opinions with however and although.

lessons.title: First conditional
lessons.goal: Talk about real future possibilities with if + present, will + verb.

explanation: Real future conditions: “If it rains, we'll stay in.” The if-clause uses present simple; the result uses will.
Order can flip, but the comma disappears: “We'll stay in if it rains.” Never will inside the if-clause.
Variations: “If it rains, we might stay in / we can stay in / let's stay in.”

examples.text: If it rains, we'll stay home.
We'll be late if the bus doesn't come.
If you help me, I'll help you.
If they don't hurry, they'll miss the train.
If I see him, I might tell him.
What will you do if it snows?

expressions.note: If it rains, we'll stay in.
I'll call you if I'm late.
If it's cheap, we might buy it.

lessons.situation: You plan an outdoor birthday with a friend: set conditions for every possible problem (rain, no bus, cold) and what you'll do in each case.

questions.prompt: It may rain. Say what you will do. (stay in)
expected: If it rains, we'll stay in.
If it rains, I'll stay in.
questions.watch: “If it will rain” — never will in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: The bus may not come. Predict lateness.
expected: If the bus doesn't come, we'll be late.
We'll be late if the bus doesn't come.
questions.watch: “If the bus won't come” — present simple after if.

questions.prompt: Offer an exchange of help.
expected: If you help me, I'll help you.
questions.watch: Both halves stay simple: present + will.

questions.prompt: Ask about a cancelled flight. (what / you / do)
expected: What will you do if the flight is cancelled?
questions.watch: will goes in the result question, not after if.

questions.prompt: Soften the result: if it's cheap, maybe buy it.
expected: If it's cheap, I might buy it.
If it's cheap, we might buy it.
questions.watch: might + base verb: “might to buy” is wrong.

questions.prompt: Say the alternative: no picnic → restaurant.
expected: If we can't have a picnic, we'll go to a restaurant.
Otherwise, we'll go to a restaurant.
questions.watch: Otherwise connects to the previous sentence's failure.

exercises.prompt: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll cancel the trip.
I'll call you if I ___ late. (be)
exercises.explain: Present simple after if: if I am late.

answers: What will you do if it snows
exercises.explain: Question word + will + you + do + if + present.

exercises.prompt: Fix: “If it will rain, we stay in.”
answers: if it rains we'll stay in
if it rains we will stay in
exercises.explain: Present after if, will in the result.

lessons.title: Relative clauses
lessons.goal: Join ideas with who, which, that and where.

explanation: who joins people, which joins things, that joins both (informal): “The woman who lives upstairs is a doctor.” “The book which won the prize…”
where joins places: “That's the café where we met.”
Shortened clauses: “The man standing there” (= who is standing). No double subject: “the book which won” not “the book which it won”.

examples.text: The woman who lives upstairs is a doctor.
It's a film which changed cinema.
The song that she wrote became famous.
That's the café where we first met.
The train (that) we caught was late.
The guy standing by the door is my cousin.

expressions.note: The person who called left a message.
the street where I grew up.
He was late, which annoyed everyone.

lessons.situation: You describe your neighbourhood to a visitor: the people who live there, the shops which are worth it and the corner where everything happens.

questions.prompt: Describe your best friend. (person who…)
expected: My best friend is the person who knows me best.
questions.watch: People take who (or that), never which.

questions.prompt: Describe an app you like. (app which…)
expected: It's an app which helps me study.
It's an app that tracks my habits.
questions.watch: Things take which or that — both are fine here.

questions.prompt: Talk about the place you grew up. (where)
expected: The town where I grew up is small.
I grew up in a village where everyone knew everyone.
questions.watch: where replaces “in which”: “the town where I grew up”.

questions.prompt: Join: “The train was late. We caught it.”
expected: The train (that) we caught was late.
questions.watch: When the joiner is the object, that can disappear.

questions.prompt: Comment on a whole fact: “He resigned, … surprised everyone.”
questions.watch: Comma + which comments on the whole idea — never “, what surprised”.

questions.prompt: Fix: “The book which it won the prize is long.”
expected: the book which won the prize is long
questions.watch: which replaces it — never both.

exercises.prompt: The woman ___ lives upstairs is a doctor.
That's the café ___ we first met.

answers: It's a film which changed cinema

exercises.prompt: Join: “He resigned. It annoyed everyone.” (use which)

lessons.title: Connectors: although, however, so
lessons.goal: Link ideas with contrast (although, however) and result (so, because).

explanation: Contrast: although + clause (“Although it was late, we went out”) and however + comma (“It was late. However, we went out.”).
Result: so joins cause → effect (“It was late, so we took a taxi”). Reason: because joins effect → cause (“We took a taxi because it was late”).
Punctuation: however needs a full stop or semicolon before it; although and because live inside the clause.

examples.text: Although it was expensive, we bought it.
We bought it. However, we regret it now.
It was raining, so we stayed in.
We stayed in because it was raining.
The film was long; nevertheless, we enjoyed it.

expressions.note: Although he's young, he leads the team.
It was full, so we left.
I left because it was full.
Even though I knew, I forgot.

lessons.situation: You and a colleague review a project: what worked, what failed, and why — connecting every point with so, because, although and however.

questions.prompt: Contrast in one sentence: it was expensive / we bought it. (although)
expected: Although it was expensive, we bought it.
questions.watch: although + full clause with a verb, not a noun.

questions.prompt: Contrast across two sentences: the plan works / it's slow. (however)
expected: The plan works. However, it's slow.
The plan works; however, it's slow.
questions.watch: however needs a stop before it: full stop or semicolon.

questions.prompt: Cause and result: the shop was full / we left. (so)
expected: The shop was full, so we left.
questions.watch: so joins cause → result with just a comma.

questions.prompt: Same idea with because.
expected: We left because the shop was full.
questions.watch: because introduces the reason: result + because + reason.

questions.prompt: Stronger contrast: you knew / you forgot. (even though)
expected: Even though I knew, I forgot.
questions.watch: Same grammar as although, stronger feeling.

questions.prompt: Contrast with a noun: the rain / we walked. (despite)
questions.watch: despite takes a noun or -ing, never a full clause.

exercises.prompt: ___ it was late, we went out.
It was raining, ___ we stayed in. (result)

answers: We left because it was full

exercises.prompt: Fix: “The plan works, however it's slow.” (punctuation)
answers: the plan works however it's slow
the plan works however it is slow
exercises.explain: However needs a stronger break: “The plan works. However, it's slow.”

lessons.title: Making suggestions
lessons.goal: Propose plans with Why don't we, How about and Let's — and accept or decline kindly.

explanation: Three openers, three grammars: Why don't we + verb (“Why don't we order pizza?”), How about + -ing (“How about watching a film?”), Let's + verb (“Let's stay in.”).
Accept: “Sounds good!” “Good idea!” Decline kindly with a reason and a counter-offer: “I'm beat, honestly. Rain check?”
Ask back with Shall we…? and What about…?: “Shall we meet at eight? What about the new place?”

examples.text: How about trying the new ramen place?

lessons.situation: Friday night, no plan: trade suggestions, accept one, decline another kindly and settle on a time and place.

questions.prompt: Suggest ordering food in. (why don't we)
questions.watch: “Why we don't order” — the inversion lives in don't we.

questions.prompt: Suggest watching a film. (how about)
questions.watch: “How about to watch” — the gerund is obligatory.

questions.prompt: Suggest staying in, directly.
questions.watch: let's + base verb: “let's to stay” is wrong.

questions.prompt: Accept a plan with enthusiasm.
questions.watch: “It sounds good” also works; “Sounds good” is the chatty form.

questions.prompt: Decline tonight, but keep the plan alive.
questions.watch: A decline without a counter-offer ends the friendship chat.

questions.prompt: Fix the time: eight.
questions.watch: shall we say + the detail.

exercises.prompt: Decline tonight kindly and keep it alive.

themes.title: The office pool
themes.subtitle: What will happen?
themes.situation: You and your colleagues bet on next week: weather, results, deadlines. Make predictions and defend them.

themes.title: The rumour mill
themes.subtitle: Who said what?
themes.situation: Office news travels fast: report what people said, and work out what is actually true.

lessons.title: Will: decisions & promises
lessons.goal: Use will for spontaneous decisions, offers, promises and predictions without evidence.

explanation: Will is for the moment of speaking: “The phone's ringing — I'll get it!” The decision happens as you talk.
It also covers promises and offers: “I'll always be there for you.” “I'll carry that for you.” And predictions without evidence: “You'll love this film.”
Contrast with going to: going to = already decided before speaking (“I'm going to study tonight”); will = decided now (“OK, I'll study with you”).
Negative: won't. Question: “Will you help me?” Never “will to help”.

examples.text: The phone's ringing — I'll get it!
examples.meaning: Decision at the moment of speaking.

examples.text: Shall I open the window? — Good idea, I'll close the door.
I'm going to study tonight. — Great, I'll join you.

lessons.situation: A friend's flat has a small crisis (broken lamp, hungry cat, empty fridge): make instant offers, promises and confident predictions as events unfold.

questions.prompt: The doorbell rings while you're both cooking. Offer to answer.
questions.watch: “I'm going to get it” sounds pre-planned — the ring is news.

questions.prompt: Promise your friend you won't be late tomorrow.
expected: I promise I won't be late.
questions.watch: “I won't to be” — won't + base verb.

questions.prompt: No evidence yet: predict your friend will love the film.
expected: You're going to love it? no — use will: You'll love it.
questions.watch: Without evidence, will is the natural choice.

questions.prompt: Offer to carry the heavy boxes.
questions.watch: “I carry them” — English needs will for the offer.

questions.prompt: Soften your prediction about tonight's traffic. (probably)
questions.watch: probably goes before will: “will probably be”.

questions.prompt: Your friend says “I'm going to clean the kitchen”. Join in spontaneously.
questions.watch: Their plan = going to; your reaction = will.

exercises.prompt: The phone's ringing — I ___ answer it.
exercises.explain: A decision at the moment of speaking takes will.
will + base verb, no evidence needed.

exercises.prompt: Your hands are full. Offer to be helped… no: offer help with the door.

lessons.title: He said he was busy
lessons.goal: Report what people said with said/thought + a tense shift back.

explanation: Direct: “I'm busy.” Reported: “He said he was busy.” The present shifts one step into the past.
Common shifts: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could, have → had. Past simple usually stays past simple.
Questions drop their question form: “Where do you live?” → “She asked where I lived.” No do/did, no inversion.

examples.text: He told me he couldn't come.
You said you liked my cooking!
I thought you were leaving today.

expressions.note: “I'm here” → she said she was there.

lessons.situation: You come back from a day off to a wall of office rumours: report who said what, and separate reliable reports from gossip.

questions.prompt: Report: “I'm leaving the company.” (Tom, to you)
expected: Tom said he was leaving the company.
Tom told me he was leaving the company.
questions.watch: “Tom said he is leaving” is possible in casual speech — the exam-safe form shifts to was.

questions.prompt: Report: “We will announce it on Friday.” (the manager)
expected: The manager said they would announce it on Friday.
questions.watch: “said they will” — shift the modal too: would.

questions.prompt: Report: “I can't find the file.” (Ana)
expected: Ana said she couldn't find the file.
Ana told me she couldn't find the file.
questions.watch: Never “said me” — say (that) or told me.

questions.prompt: Report the question: “Where do you work?”
questions.watch: No did, no inversion: “asked where did I work” is wrong.

questions.prompt: Pass on gossip about the merger. (People are saying…)
expected: People are saying the merger is off.
People are saying there's going to be a merger.
questions.watch: are saying keeps it vague and deniable.

questions.prompt: Correct a rumour: “I thought you were leaving, but you're not.”
expected: I thought you were leaving, but you're still here.
I thought you were leaving — obviously not!
questions.watch: thought + was for the belief you had.

exercises.explain: say (that) + clause; tell needs a person: told ME.

exercises.prompt: They said they ___ call later. (will → shift)
Report this question. (asked / I / where / she / lived)
Fix: “He said me he is busy.”
answers: he told me he was busy
exercises.explain: said me doesn't exist; and is shifts to was.

lessons.title: Phrasal verbs you already use
lessons.goal: Master the ten everyday phrasal verbs that replace formal verbs in speech.

explanation: A phrasal verb = verb + particle with its own meaning: get up (leave the bed), give up (stop trying), look for (search). The particle changes everything.
Separable or not: “turn it off” (separable — the pronoun goes in the middle, never at the end). “Look after the cat” (inseparable). Learn each verb's habit.
Formal English often has a single-verb twin: find out = discover, put off = postpone. Speech prefers the phrasal; writing accepts both.

examples.text: I get up at six even on Sundays.
Turn it off and back on again.
Can you look after the cat this weekend?
I found out the truth yesterday.

expressions.note: turn it on, never turn on it.
I'll find out and tell you.

lessons.situation: A friend is moving house: phrasal verbs everywhere — get up early, pick up boxes, look after the dog, give up the sofa, turn off the lights.

questions.prompt: Say what time you leave the bed on Mondays.
expected: I get up at <time> on Mondays.
questions.watch: “I get me up” — no pronoun: I get up.

questions.prompt: Encourage a friend who wants to quit the gym to continue.
questions.watch: give up alone works: no object needed.

questions.prompt: Ask someone to take care of your dog this weekend.
expected: Can you look after my dog this weekend?
questions.watch: look after ≠ look for (search).

questions.prompt: The pronoun goes in the middle: the lights / turn off / them.
questions.watch: “Turn off them” is wrong — pronouns sit inside.

questions.prompt: Say you discovered the truth yesterday. (phrasal)
expected: I found out the truth yesterday.
questions.watch: found out, not “found up” or “discovered out”.

questions.prompt: Say the meeting was postponed. (phrasal)
questions.watch: put off + thing; put the meeting off also works.

lessons.title: Second conditional
lessons.goal: Imagine unreal presents and alternatives with if + past, would + verb.

explanation: Unreal presents use if + past simple, would + verb: “If I had more time, I would learn the piano.” The time is now/forward — the past form only marks unreality.
Questions: “What would you do if you lost your job?” I'd = I would.
Softer advice uses would in the result: “If I were you, I'd negotiate.” Note the fixed phrase If I were you.

examples.text: If I won the lottery, I would travel for a year.
If I were you, I'd ask for a raise.
Would you move abroad if you got the chance?
I wouldn't say that if I weren't sure.
If we had a bigger budget, we could hire help.
Compare: “If it rains, we'll stay” (real) vs “If it rained, we'd stay” (unlikely).

expressions.note: If I had time, I would cook.
were, not was, in formal English.
I'd never lie to a client.

expressions.meaning: Ability or possibility in the result.
expressions.note: If we left now, we could catch it.
If I win… (possible) vs If I won… (fantasy).

lessons.situation: A debate table: what would you do with a year off, a sudden fortune, a job abroad? Defend your hypotheticals and challenge theirs.

questions.prompt: Imagine you had a year off. What would you do?
expected: If I had a year off, I would <activity>.
questions.watch: “If I would have a year” — never would in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: Give advice to a friend who earns too little. (If I were you…)
expected: If I were you, I'd ask for a raise.
If I were you, I would look for another job.
questions.watch: The fixed advice formula uses were.

questions.prompt: Ask about your friend's hypothetical move abroad.
expected: Would you move abroad if you got the chance?
questions.watch: would in the result question; past in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: Say what is possible, not certain: if we left now / catch the train.
expected: If we left now, we could catch the train.
questions.watch: could replaces would for possibility.

questions.prompt: Contrast real vs imaginary: rain tomorrow / money for a trip.
expected: If it rains tomorrow, we'll cancel. If I had money for a trip, I'd go today.
questions.watch: Real future takes present+will; fantasy takes past+would.

questions.prompt: Firm unreal negative: lie to a client.
expected: I'd never lie to a client.
I would never lie to a client.
questions.watch: would + never + base verb.

If I were you, I ___ ask for a raise.
exercises.explain: would in the result: I'd ask.

exercises.prompt: Ask the hypothetical question. (move / would / if / you / abroad / the chance / you / got)
answers: Would you move abroad if you got the chance

answers: if i had time i would cook
exercises.explain: The if-clause takes had, never would have.

lessons.title: The passive: reporting
lessons.goal: Report information with is/are/was/were + past participle when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

explanation: Passive = be + past participle: “The bridge was built in 1900.” “These shoes are made in Portugal.” The doer disappears or moves to a by-phrase.
Use it when the doer is obvious, unknown or unimportant — the classic register of news, reports and instructions.
Questions and negatives behave like be: “Was it built recently?” “It isn't sold here.”

examples.text: The results will be published tomorrow.
These shoes are made in Portugal.
The novel was written by a nurse.
Payment must be made in advance.

expressions.note: The report will be shared on Monday.
It is said that the lake is bottomless.

lessons.situation: You present a short report about your town's history: what was built, what is produced there and what will be opened next year.

questions.prompt: Report a past fact: they built the theatre in 1921. (passive)
questions.watch: “was build” — the participle is built.

questions.prompt: State a present fact: they make these shoes in Portugal. (passive)
expected: These shoes are made in Portugal.
questions.watch: “are make” — participle, not base form.

questions.prompt: Announce a plan: they will publish the results tomorrow. (passive)
expected: The results will be published tomorrow.
questions.watch: “will published” — be comes first: will be published.

questions.prompt: State a rule: you must validate tickets. (passive)
questions.watch: Modal + be + participle.

questions.prompt: The doer matters here. Join: “Shakespeare wrote Hamlet.” Keep Shakespeare. (passive)
questions.watch: by appears only when the doer is important information.

questions.prompt: Ask about a past event in passive form. (the email / send)
questions.watch: be moves to the front: Was it sent?

answers: Tickets must be validated before boarding

lessons.title: Negotiating
lessons.goal: Negotiate politely: propose conditions, concede ground and close a deal.

explanation: Proposals soften with could/would: “Could we possibly move the deadline?” “Would it help if I took the night shift?”
Concede with a condition: “That works if…”, “As long as…, I'm happy to…”. Push back without conflict: “I see your point, however…”
Close: “Shall we say…?”, “So we agree on…”, “I think we have a deal.”

examples.text: Could we possibly start at ten?
That works if the report arrives on Thursday.
As long as I keep Fridays free, I'm happy to travel.
I see your point; however, the budget is fixed.
What if we split the difference?

expressions.note: As long as costs stay under X.
What if we split the costs?

lessons.situation: You negotiate a remote-work arrangement with your manager: propose, concede, push back once and close with a concrete deal.

questions.prompt: Politely propose a later start time.
expected: Could we possibly start at ten?
Would it be possible to start later?
questions.watch: Bare commands sound abrupt in negotiation; use could/would.

questions.prompt: Accept travelling, with one condition. (as long as)
expected: That works as long as I keep Fridays free.
As long as costs are covered, I'm happy to travel.
questions.watch: as long as + present simple for your condition.

questions.prompt: Disagree respectfully with a tight deadline.
expected: I see your point; however, the deadline is too tight.
I understand, however we need two more days.
questions.watch: Acknowledge first — however lands softer after agreement words.

questions.prompt: Offer a middle ground on price.
expected: What if we split the difference?
What if we meet in the middle?
questions.watch: what if + present simple proposes the path.

questions.prompt: Close the deal on a number. (thirty percent)
questions.watch: shall we say + the final number.

questions.prompt: State the deal you both reached.
expected: So we agree on: remote Mondays and a Thursday report.
So we agree: I travel twice a month, you cover the costs.
questions.watch: Good negotiators summarise: “So we agree on…”.

exercises.prompt: ___ we possibly move the meeting to Thursday?
exercises.explain: Could we possibly…? is the softest proposal.

exercises.prompt: That works ___ ___ as the budget is approved. (2 words: condition)
exercises.explain: as long as / so long as = siempre que.

answers: I see your point however the budget is fixed

exercises.prompt: Close a deal at ten percent.
exercises.explain: Shall we say + number closes it.
