lessons.title: Register: formal vs informal
lessons.goal: Rephrase the same message for different audiences and levels of formality.

explanation: Informal leans on phrasal verbs and contractions: “We'll set up a call.” Formal prefers single verbs: “We will arrange a call.”
Requests climb the ladder of politeness: “Send it” → “Can you send it?” → “Could you send it?” → “I would be grateful if you could send it.”
Written formality also changes vocabulary: get → receive, help → assistance, but → however, kids → children.

examples.text: We'll set up a call tomorrow. (informal)
We will arrange a call tomorrow. (formal)
I would be grateful if you could send the invoice.
Sorry, that doesn't work for me. (informal)
Unfortunately, that arrangement is not feasible. (formal)

expressions.text: I would be grateful if you could …
Sorry about that → I apologise for the inconvenience.

lessons.situation: One message, three rooms: say the same cancellation to a friend, then to a client, then in a formal complaint — and feel the register move.

questions.prompt: Say informally that you'll organise a call.
questions.watch: Phrasal verbs + contractions are the informal markers.

questions.prompt: Now say it formally. (arrange)
questions.watch: Single verb, no contraction.

questions.prompt: Make this formal: “Can you send the report?”
expected: I would be grateful if you could send the report.
Could you please send the report?
questions.watch: would be grateful is the top rung for email.

questions.prompt: Refuse formally: the arrangement doesn't work.
expected: Unfortunately, that arrangement is not feasible.
Unfortunately, we are unable to accept the arrangement.
questions.watch: Formal refusals start with unfortunately and avoid contractions.

questions.prompt: Make this formal: “Sorry about the delay.”
expected: Please accept my apologies for the delay.
questions.watch: Match formality to the damage.

questions.prompt: Spot the register: “We received your message” vs “We got your message”.
expected: we received your message is formal
we got your message is informal
questions.watch: Same meaning; receive belongs to formal writing.

options: I would be grateful if you could reply.
answers: I would be grateful if you could reply.
exercises.explain: would be grateful marks formal register.

lessons.title: Natural chunks
lessons.goal: Replace literal sentences with natural chunks and idioms — precisely, not decoratively.

explanation: Chunks are ready-made phrases native speakers reach for: “It depends.” “That makes sense.” “As far as I know…” “I'm not sure about that.”
Idioms carry culture and risk: “It's a grey area” is safe and useful; rare or dated idioms can sound costume-y. One per conversation is plenty.
Upgrading literal speech: “I don't decide yet” → “I'm still on the fence.” The chunk must match the meaning exactly.

examples.text: As far as I know, the flight is on time.
It's a bit of a grey area.
examples.meaning: Not clearly one thing or the other.

expressions.note: The law here is a grey area.

lessons.situation: You coach a colleague before a difficult meeting: swap their literal lines for natural chunks — and decide which idioms to avoid.

questions.prompt: Answer naturally when asked if remote work is better.
questions.watch: “It depends of” — English takes on.

questions.prompt: Confirm you understood the explanation.
questions.watch: Never “it has sense” — the chunk is makes sense.

questions.prompt: Soften a claim about tomorrow's schedule.
expected: As far as I know, it's free.
As far as I know, the schedule hasn't changed.
questions.watch: The chunk admits your knowledge might be incomplete.

questions.prompt: Say you haven't decided between the two offers.
questions.watch: The fence sits between two options — that's the image.

questions.prompt: Say the rule is unclear. (idiom)
expected: It's a bit of a grey area.
questions.watch: grey (BrE) or gray (AmE) — both fine.

questions.prompt: Say you'll decide as things happen. (idiom)
questions.watch: ear, not year — it comes from music.

exercises.explain: On the fence = between two options, undecided.

exercises.prompt: Soften your claim about the flight.
answers: As far as I know the flight is on time
exercises.explain: as far as I know + the claim.

lessons.title: Hedging & precision
lessons.goal: Fine-tune opinions: soften, intensify and qualify like a confident speaker.

explanation: Hedging protects accuracy: “tends to”, “to some extent”, “arguably”, “in most cases”. Strong claims need strong evidence — otherwise hedge.
Intensifiers scale: slightly < rather < considerably < far. “Far more efficient” is stronger than “slightly more efficient”.
Precision beats intensity: “a threefold increase” > “a lot more”. Numbers, examples and scope (“in this case”) make opinions defensible.

examples.text: This approach tends to work better.
Arguably, it's the best option on the table.
The new version is far more stable.
Costs fell by roughly a third.
In this specific case, I'd wait.

expressions.note: Prices tend to rise in summer.

expressions.text: to some extent / to a degree

expressions.note: Arguably the best paella in town.

lessons.situation: You present an opinion to a skeptical audience: claim, hedge, quantify and limit scope — then defend it once challenged.

questions.prompt: Hedge a claim about remote productivity.
expected: Remote work tends to increase productivity.
It tends to work better for focused tasks.
questions.watch: tends to + base verb softens the pattern without killing it.

questions.prompt: Agree, but only partly.
questions.watch: The quantifier keeps the disagreement alive.

questions.prompt: Give a defensible superlative opinion about a restaurant.
expected: Arguably, it's the best ramen in the city.
questions.watch: arguably signals: I can defend this.

questions.prompt: Rank the intensifiers: slightly / far / rather. (weakest to strongest)
questions.watch: slightly < rather < considerably < far.

questions.prompt: Be precise about a cost drop: from 90 to 60. (roughly)
expected: Costs fell by roughly a third.
questions.watch: roughly + fraction beats “a lot less”.

questions.prompt: Limit your advice so it isn't universal.
expected: In this specific case, I'd wait.
In this case, I'd wait before deciding.
questions.watch: in this case protects the advice from other contexts.

exercises.prompt: Which claim is the most hedged?
exercises.explain: tends to is the hedged pattern claim.

exercises.prompt: The new engine is ___ more efficient. (strongest intensifier)
exercises.explain: far (or considerably) is stronger than slightly.
depend on — the preposition is on.

lessons.title: The academic voice
lessons.goal: State positions in academic and professional registers: impersonal, evidenced, measured.

explanation: The academic voice removes the “I”: “This paper argues that…”, “The data suggests…”, “It has been observed that…”. The claim carries the sentence, not the person.
Evidence verbs scale certainty: demonstrate > suggest > indicate > appear to. Choose the verb that matches the strength of your data.
Structure is visible: “First… Second… Taken together, these findings…” — the reader should always know where they are.

examples.text: This paper argues that hybrid models outperform either extreme.
The data suggests a modest effect.
The results demonstrate a clear correlation.
It has been observed that remote teams innovate differently.
Taken together, these findings point to a structural cause.
Further research is needed to confirm the effect.

expressions.note: Ends the middle, opens the close.

lessons.situation: You present a controversial finding to a skeptical panel: thesis, evidence verbs that match your data, visible structure and an honest limit.

questions.prompt: State your thesis formally. (hybrid models outperform)
expected: This paper argues that hybrid models outperform either extreme.
questions.watch: argues that + full clause — the position, not the topic.

questions.prompt: Your evidence is moderate. Choose the verb. (the data / a modest effect)
expected: The data suggests a modest effect.
questions.watch: demonstrates would overclaim; suggests is honest.

questions.prompt: Your evidence is strong. Choose the verb. (clear correlation)
expected: The results demonstrate a clear correlation.
questions.watch: With strong data, demonstrates is the honest choice.

questions.prompt: Report an observation without saying who observed it.
expected: It has been observed that remote teams innovate differently.
questions.watch: It + has been + participle keeps the voice out.

questions.prompt: Synthesise two findings into one conclusion.
expected: Taken together, these findings point to a structural cause.
questions.watch: Taken together announces the synthesis.

questions.prompt: Close with the honest limit of the study.
expected: Further research is needed to confirm the effect.
questions.watch: Every credible study admits its edge.

exercises.prompt: The data ___ a modest effect. (moderate evidence)
exercises.explain: Moderate evidence takes suggests, not demonstrates.

exercises.prompt: It has ___ observed that remote teams innovate differently.

answers: This paper argues that hybrid models outperform either extreme
further research is needed to confirm the effect
